title: Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture

concept.text: The innovation would reliably close a spontaneously ruptured fetal membrane and sustain restoration of the amniotic fluid compartment around the fetus. Its intended function is to preserve an existing pregnancy by repairing the compartment in which development continues. Success would require durable fluid restoration and better clinical outcomes, rather than an isolated observation of sealing or a temporary increase in fluid.

Preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, or PPROM, means that the membranes rupture before labor and before term. Membrane sealing and fluid restoration have been investigated through amniopatch procedures. The retained PubMed record documents one such investigation in spontaneous PPROM, but the article is retracted and cannot establish treatment efficacy. The proposed innovation therefore remains a target capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that reliable restoration is currently available.

significance.text: If effective, restoration would add a direct way to preserve the pregnancy's amniotic compartment while allowing development to continue toward a safer gestation. ACOG frames management after membrane rupture around gestational age and the competing risks of delivery and continued pregnancy, including infection, placental abruption and umbilical cord accident. These are risks, not inevitable consequences of rupture. A repair would be clinically consequential only if its benefits outweighed the risks of the intervention and of prolonging pregnancy.

Conditional significance: sustained fluid restoration could create an opportunity for better lung and limb development, less pulmonary hypoplasia and improved survival. These are intended downstream benefits requiring direct evidence; sealing alone does not demonstrate them. Previable and periviable rupture are proposed priority populations because preserving additional developmental time could be especially consequential there. The retained texts do not establish their prognosis, quantify the expected benefit, or show how benefit would differ across gestational ages.

Conceptual limits: restoring the compartment addresses a different problem from suppressing contractions or controlling the timing of birth. Changing labor timing does not itself demonstrate membrane closure or fluid restoration, and repairing membranes would not establish control over every cause of premature delivery. The innovation also does not require complete artificial gestation: its purpose is to repair part of the environment supporting an ongoing pregnancy within the uterus.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reproducible closure of a spontaneous membrane defect with sustained restoration of amniotic fluid and acceptable maternal and fetal safety. The research identifies limited membrane healing, continuing leakage and ascending infection as candidate obstacles. Those explanations remain hypotheses within this record: the retained evidence does not establish the biological healing deficit, the operative leakage mechanism or the ascending route of infection. ACOG supports infection as a clinical risk, but does not, in the retained abstract, establish these specific repair barriers.

Proposed engineering requirements include delivering a repair to the defect without causing additional injury, maintaining closure long enough for fluid to remain restored, and determining whether the intervention changes infection risk. A convincing method would need to distinguish the repair's effect from fluid replacement or spontaneous changes in fluid volume. It would also need evidence specifically in spontaneous rupture: success after a procedure-related needle puncture would demonstrate a narrower capability and would not establish efficacy for spontaneous PPROM.

The clinical breakthrough extends beyond making a seal. A method must show that the additional time in pregnancy produces meaningful neonatal benefit without an unacceptable increase in maternal harm. ACOG's delivery-versus-expectancy framework makes this tradeoff central. The supplied records do not establish whether any current restorative treatment has met it or changed clinical practice.

current_state.text: ACOG Practice Bulletin 217 was issued in March 2020, and the retained landing page identifies it as reaffirmed in 2026. Its abstract states that preterm PROM affects approximately 2–3% of pregnancies in the United States and accounts for a significant proportion of preterm births. The available material is the landing page and abstract, not the full bulletin; it supports this clinical context but does not provide a comprehensive assessment of membrane-repair treatments.

The supplied research attributes to a 2016 Cochrane review a conclusion that evidence was insufficient to evaluate sealing procedures for PPROM, and describes two small trials with bias concerns that did not establish perinatal benefit. No source text for that review was retained. Its conclusions, trial count and quality assessment therefore remain unverified in this record and cannot serve as a confirmed summary of the evidence.

The research also attributes to a 2022 amniopatch meta-analysis fluid reaccumulation in 26% of spontaneous cases and 53% of iatrogenic cases, together with a call for trials. The source text and author list were not retained, so these percentages, their denominators, definitions and interpretation cannot be verified here. They are preserved as unresolved reported figures, rather than established success rates. Even if confirmed, fluid reaccumulation would need to be distinguished from durable closure and improved maternal or neonatal outcomes.

The retained PubMed abstract for a randomized amniopatch trial in spontaneous PPROM, involving women at 24–34 weeks, historically reported complete sealing in 6 of 50 treated women, or 12%, and none of the controls. The same record marks the article as retracted and lists a retraction published online on April 7, 2026. These numbers describe what the abstract reported; they are not reliable evidence of efficacy. The substantive explanation for the retraction was not supplied, so no conclusion about its particular cause is warranted.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material establishes the clinical problem and historical investigation of repair, but does not establish reliable restoration after spontaneous rupture or comprehensively describe treatment availability as of November 1, 2026. The supplied search record is empty. The 2026 reaffirmation and retraction provide specific dated information, not a complete contemporary treatment survey. Missing review texts do not show that their reported findings are false, and uncertainty about current availability does not invalidate the repair concept.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: a prospective comparative study in spontaneous PPROM would show sustained restoration of normal amniotic fluid, meaningful pregnancy prolongation, reduced pulmonary hypoplasia and lower perinatal mortality compared with contemporaneous expectant care, without an increase in serious maternal infection. These are proposed criteria for a convincing advance, not established standards or a claim of feasibility. Reaching a particular gestational age would not by itself demonstrate that pulmonary hypoplasia had been avoided; pulmonary outcomes must be measured directly.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained normal fluid restoration improves outcomes in spontaneous PPROM

completion_criteria.text: The study should prespecify fluid measurements and the reference used to define normality, the duration required for restoration, how closure and recurrent leakage will be assessed, gestational-age strata, pulmonary and survival outcomes, and maternal safety assessment. It should identify when continued pregnancy becomes unsafe and how those events count in the analysis. This proposal reflects the need to assess both delivery risks and risks of continued pregnancy described in the ACOG abstract; the detailed study requirements are a synthesis rather than source-endorsed thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Study prespecifies restoration criteria, clinical outcomes and maternal safety assessment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: results should be replicated independently across centers, with transparent accounting of eligible patients, failures, repeat interventions and adverse outcomes. Spontaneous and iatrogenic rupture should be analyzed separately, and results should identify the gestational ages and clinical circumstances in which the method works. A temporary fluid increase or success predominantly after needle injury would not meet the proposed spontaneous-rupture objective. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within tested populations, not universal repair across every membrane defect or pregnancy.
completion_criteria.label: Independent multicenter replication reports full outcomes and demonstrated clinical scope

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock: both could prolong pregnancy, but they act on different targets. OBG-01 concerns the causal timing of labor; OBG-10 concerns membrane integrity and the amniotic fluid compartment. Either capability could complement the other, while neither alone establishes the other's function.

Conceptual comparison with OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, and OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression: these address alternative systems or organs for supporting gestation. OBG-10 repairs an existing compartment within an ongoing uterine pregnancy. Shared developmental goals do not make membrane repair equivalent to extrauterine support, complete artificial gestation or manufacturing a uterus.

Conceptual comparison with OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency, and OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease: all seek benefit during an ongoing pregnancy, but the intervention targets differ. Placental function, fetal molecular disease and membrane integrity are distinct problems. Repairing one does not demonstrate correction of the others, although combined capabilities could potentially benefit pregnancies with more than one condition.

Conceptual comparison with OBG-02, Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell; OBG-05, Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging; OBG-07, A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis; and OBG-09, Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma: these concern gamete production, ovarian aging, endometriosis or cancer interception with fertility preservation. Their broad overlap is reproductive health. Their targets and demonstrations remain distinct from restoring the amniotic compartment after rupture.

unresolved_issues: The 2016 Cochrane review's conclusions, trial count and bias assessment remain unverified because its text was not retained.
The 2022 meta-analysis's 26% and 53% figures, denominators, outcome definitions, follow-up duration and author identity remain unverified.
The substantive reason for the amniopatch trial's retraction is not supplied.
The biological basis and relative importance of limited healing, continuing leakage and ascending infection require evidence beyond the retained texts.
The supplied material does not establish current repair availability or whether any restorative treatment has changed practice as of November 1, 2026.
Expected benefits, prognosis and intervention risks across previable, periviable and later gestational ages remain unquantified in this record.
Fluid-restoration duration, clinically meaningful benefit thresholds, safety margins and suitable eligibility boundaries would need prospective justification.

brief.title: Repairing the waters around a developing baby
possible: When the membranes holding fluid around a baby break before labor and too early in pregnancy, a repair could close the tear and keep the fluid restored. This could allow the pregnancy to continue while the baby develops in the uterus.
why: More time with fluid around the baby could support lung and limb development, reduce dangerously underdeveloped lungs and improve survival. The opportunity could matter especially when the waters break very early in pregnancy.

sources.who: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
sources.showed: Their clinical guidance describes how decisions after the waters break depend on the stage of pregnancy and the competing risks of delivery and continuing pregnancy, including infection.
sources.cited_for: Repair must be judged against the risks of both early delivery and continuing pregnancy.
sources.not_established: The guidance does not establish that membrane repair safely restores fluid and improves outcomes.

sources.showed: This review assesses procedures intended to seal membranes after the waters break before labor and before term.
sources.cited_for: It addresses membrane sealing as a possible treatment.
sources.not_established: Reliable closure with sustained fluid restoration and better outcomes remains unestablished.

sources.showed: This combined analysis of studies examines amniopatch, a procedure intended to seal ruptured membranes, and the return of fluid.
sources.cited_for: It addresses fluid returning after a membrane-sealing procedure.
sources.not_established: Fluid returning does not establish durable closure or better outcomes for mothers and babies.

sources.showed: A now-retracted trial reported membrane sealing and an increase in the amniotic fluid index (AFI), a measure of fluid around the fetus, after a patch procedure.
sources.quote: Women in the amniopatch group showed a significant increase of AFI compared to controls
sources.cited_for: The trial illustrates clinical investigation of repair after spontaneous membrane rupture.
sources.not_established: The retracted trial cannot establish that the procedure works or is safe.

shown: Ahmed M Maged and colleagues reported membrane sealing and increased fluid after a patch procedure in pregnancies where the waters broke spontaneously. Their trial was retracted, so its findings cannot establish treatment effectiveness. Reliable, lasting restoration with better clinical outcomes remains unproven.
missing: A repair must reliably close spontaneous tears and sustain fluid restoration without causing additional injury.
Studies must distinguish the repair's effect from fluid replacement or spontaneous changes in fluid volume.
Longer pregnancy must improve babies' lung development and survival without unacceptable harm to mothers.

milestones.label: Lasting fluid restoration improves outcomes after spontaneous rupture
milestones.explanation: A comparative study would have to show lasting normal fluid, longer pregnancy, fewer underdeveloped lungs and deaths around birth, without more serious maternal infection. This would establish benefit beyond sealing.

milestones.label: Studies define restoration, outcomes and safety before starting
milestones.explanation: A study would have to predefine normal fluid, restoration duration, leakage checks, pregnancy-stage groups, lung and survival outcomes, and maternal safety and stopping rules. This would make benefits and harms interpretable.

milestones.label: Independent centers reproduce results and establish who benefits
milestones.explanation: Independent centers would have to reproduce benefits, report failures, repeat repairs and harms, and separate spontaneous from procedure-related rupture by pregnancy stage. This would establish reproducibility and clinical scope.

uncertain: The relative roles of limited membrane healing, continuing leakage and infection in preventing successful repair remain unclear.
The balance of benefit and harm may differ with the stage of pregnancy and clinical circumstances.
How long fluid must stay restored, and what benefit and safety thresholds would justify treatment, remain open questions.

page.title: Fetal membrane repair after spontaneous PPROM
page.definition: A treatment closes spontaneously ruptured fetal membranes and maintains the fluid surrounding the fetus, with demonstrated neonatal benefit and maternal safety. Preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM) means rupture before labor and before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy.

goal.need: ACOG’s March 2020 bulletin reports that PPROM complicates approximately 2–3% of pregnancies in the United States. For rupture around the limit of viability, it reports maternal sepsis in approximately 1–5% of cases. Repair therefore requires evidence of neonatal benefit alongside maternal safety; retaining fluid alone does not resolve this clinical tradeoff.

statements.body: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists
statements.quote: The probability of neonatal death and morbidity associated with PROM decreases with longer latency and advancing gestational age
statements.context: The passage concerns periviable rupture. Latency is the interval between membrane rupture and delivery.

statements.quote: with an effort to seal the ruptured membranes using the amniopatch technique.
statements.context: The registered randomized study enrolled 100 women with spontaneous PPROM at 24–34 weeks. Its associated efficacy publication was subsequently retracted.

statements.quote: serial amnioinfusions and amniopatch are considered investigational and should be used only in a clinical trial setting
statements.context: Consult Series 71 addresses previable and periviable PPROM and is endorsed by ACOG.

completion.title: SMFM or RCOG recommends membrane repair for routine care after spontaneous PPROM.
completion.criterion: SMFM or RCOG publishes a clinical guideline recommending a membrane-repair treatment for routine use in a defined spontaneous-PPROM population. The recommendation must concern sustained cessation of leakage and restoration of amniotic fluid, supported by controlled evidence of neonatal benefit and assessment of maternal harms. A recommendation confined to clinical trials does not pass.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback, anchored to SMFM’s investigational-only recommendation and RCOG’s description of the treatment gap; neither society has published this completion test.
completion.basis: Searches of ACOG Practice Bulletin 217, SMFM Consult Series 71, RCOG guidance, ClinicalTrials.gov and FDA material found no published completion criterion combining durable repair, neonatal benefit and maternal safety. Routine-care endorsement is an observable fallback consistent with the societies’ present distinction between experimental procedures and recommended treatment.

milestones.title: A repair seals a 3.5 mm human fetal-membrane puncture during a 10-minute laboratory leakage test.
milestones.criterion: Fresh human fetal membranes are punctured with a 3.5 mm trocar, repaired, stretched by approximately 30% of their original area two minutes after treatment, and covered with 0.3 L water for 10 minutes without leakage. The published experiment achieved closure in all three test cases. This establishes laboratory sealing of a manufactured defect.
milestones.set_by: Bilic et al., published experimental protocol; developed for iatrogenic punctures rather than spontaneous PPROM.
milestones.threshold_quote: To demonstrate leak-proof sealing, the stretched membranes, still mounted in the device, were overlaid for 10 min with 0.3 L water.

milestones.title: Repaired fetal-membrane punctures show no leakage at examination 10–12 days later in pregnant sheep.
milestones.criterion: Repair a defect made with a 10 French trocar in pregnant sheep and find no leakage by visual inspection during the study’s fluid-tracer test before explantation at 10–12 days. The experiment placed 10 implants in eight uterine horns of five ewes; all implant sites were sealed, all five ewes survived, and 10 of 11 fetuses survived. It did not test spontaneous rupture.
milestones.set_by: Avilla-Royo et al., published sheep-model protocol; the defects were surgically created and treated under direct vision.
milestones.threshold_quote: All implants were tight at explantation, and no AF leakage was observed in any of them.

milestones.title: An amniopatch completely seals a spontaneous membrane rupture in a pregnant patient.
milestones.criterion: Complete sealing after an amniopatch meets the published clinical success criterion. Kwak et al. reported this result in one of seven women with spontaneous rupture diagnosed at 17–23 weeks; that patient delivered at 39 weeks. The comparison group comprised 22 conservatively managed pregnancies. Overall neonatal outcomes were similar between groups, so this observation does not establish treatment efficacy.
milestones.set_by: Kwak et al., published success classification in a retrospective spontaneous-PPROM cohort; not a society standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: Amniopatch treatment was successful in 1 of 7 cases (14.3%), in which the ruptured membranes were completely sealed

milestones.title: Amniotic fluid rises above the gestational-age 10th percentile one week after treatment of spontaneous PPROM.
milestones.criterion: Achieve the registered primary outcome of NCT03473210: an amniotic fluid index above the 10th percentile for gestational age one week after the procedure. The index is an ultrasound measure of fluid around the fetus. The randomized study enrolled 100 women at 24–34 weeks and excluded iatrogenic rupture. Its associated publication was retracted on 7 April 2026; that publication cannot establish that this milestone was reached.
milestones.set_by: Cairo University, NCT03473210 primary-outcome table; the threshold and assessment time appear only in that table.

milestones.title: A randomized study establishes neonatal benefit and maternal safety from sustained repair of spontaneous PPROM.
milestones.criterion: A prospective randomized comparison with standard care meets its registered neonatal efficacy endpoint and maternal safety criterion while demonstrating cessation of leakage and maintained fluid restoration over its prespecified follow-up. The clinical outcomes must include perinatal mortality and maternal infection. No universal minimum effect size, restoration duration or maternal safety margin was found; those values must come from the study’s protocol rather than an Atlas numerical threshold.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback after searches of clinical guidance and trial registrations found no combined efficacy-and-safety pass criterion; Cochrane specifies relevant outcomes but no numerical success threshold.

not_found: No published society, regulator or registered-protocol criterion was found that defines completion through a specified duration of repair, neonatal effect size and maternal safety margin.
No mandatory membrane-repair-specific preclinical threshold or regulatory development sequence was found.
The publisher’s full text of the 2022 amniopatch meta-analysis could not be opened; its accessible abstract did not establish restoration duration or outcome-specific denominators.
The publisher’s retraction notice could not be opened; its PubMed record confirms the retraction and its publication date.

results.detail: The report concerns spontaneous PPROM, but the article was retracted, so its finding does not establish the milestone.
results.quote: Amniopatch was successful in complete sealing of the membrane defect in 6/50 (12%) of women while none the control group have undergone similar sealing

results.finding: A randomized trial of 100 women reported complete sealing in 6 of 50 amniopatch recipients.
results.detail: The abstract does not report a registered neonatal efficacy endpoint, perinatal mortality, maternal infection, or sustained restoration over prespecified follow-up. The article was retracted.
results.quote: Amniopatch was successful in complete sealing of the membrane defect in 6/50 (12%) of women while none the control group have undergone similar sealing

results.finding: cPEG sealed 3.5 mm punctures in all 3 human fetal-membrane test cases.
results.detail: Fresh membranes were stretched approximately 30% two minutes after treatment, then covered with 0.3 L of water for 10 minutes. The seal remained leak-proof.
results.quote: Successful closure was achieved in all three test cases. Application of cPEG tissue adhesive over the defect resulted in an immediate leak-proof membrane seal that remained functional upon further radial stretch of the membranes.

results.finding: Among 7 women with spontaneous previable PPROM treated with amniopatch, 1 had complete membrane sealing.
results.detail: Rupture was diagnosed at 17–23 weeks. The patient delivered at 39 weeks; overall neonatal outcomes were similar to those in 22 conservatively managed pregnancies.
results.quote: Amniopatch treatment was successful in 1 of 7 cases (14.3%), in which the ruptured membranes were completely sealed and the patient delivered a healthy baby at 39 weeks' gestation.

results.finding: cPEG sealed trocar punctures in all 3 human fetal membrane test cases.
results.detail: The test used isolated human membranes in vitro and assessed immediate sealing under stretch; it did not examine pregnant sheep or sealing after 10–12 days.
results.quote: Successful closure was achieved in all three test cases. Application of cPEG tissue adhesive over the defect resulted in an immediate leak-proof membrane seal that remained functional upon further radial stretch of the membranes.

results.finding: Amniopatch sealed spontaneous PPROM in 1 of 7 treated women.
results.detail: This retrospective comparison with 22 conservatively managed controls did not establish the registered neonatal efficacy and maternal safety outcomes in a randomized study or demonstrate sustained fluid restoration.
